name: Gnathang
tagline: A high yak valley on the Silk Route, scene of the 1888 fighting
meta_description: Gnathang (Nathang) valley on the Silk Route: 1888 war memorials, the old Baba Mandir, yak pastures, homestay prices, permits and altitude advice.
summary: Gnathang, also written Nathang, is a high valley at about 3,800–4,000 m on the Silk Route, about 23 km above Zuluk. A village of 13 households, it has yak pastures, a small monastery, memorials of the 1888 war and simple homestays at ₹1,200–2,000 with meals. It needs a Silk Route permit and a sound night lower down first.

local_story.title: A grazing ground that became a battlefield
paras: Gnathang is a broad, grassy bowl in the high country between Zuluk and Kupup, on the old trade road from Kalimpong to Jelep La. For centuries it was summer grazing for yak herders, and a halt for mule trains climbing towards the pass. The 2011 census counted just 13 households and 60 people in Gnathang village, and in winter, when snow lies deep, it is even quieter.

In 1888 the valley became a battlefield. Tibetan troops had built a fort at Lingtu, inside what the British regarded as Sikkim, and in March 1888 a British force drove them out. On 22 May 1888 Tibetan forces attacked the British position at Gnathang and were driven back. Later that year the British pushed on over Jelep La. The Anglo-Chinese Convention of 1890 then fixed the Sikkim–Tibet border along the watershed. Memorials along this stretch of road, including in the Tukla valley nearby, recall the soldiers who died.

Gnathang's later story is the army's. After the border closed in 1962 the valley filled with camps, and the original shrine of Sepoy Harbhajan Singh, who died near Nathu La on 4 October 1968, stands as a bunker on this side of the ridge, now called the old Baba Mandir. Families in the village keep yaks, run a few homestays and look after the small monastery. In 2021 Gnathang became part of Sikkim's new Pakyong district.

did_you_know: The 2011 census counted 13 households and 60 people in Gnathang village, which covers about 16 hectares of the valley floor.
On 22 May 1888 Tibetan forces attacked the British post at Gnathang during the Sikkim expedition, which ended with the 1890 Anglo-Chinese Convention fixing the border.
The old Baba Mandir near Gnathang is the original bunker shrine of Sepoy Harbhajan Singh; the newer shrine on the Nathu La road was built in 1982.
intro: Gnathang is where the Silk Route leaves the forest behind. Beyond Lungthung the road crests a ridge and drops into an open valley of grass, low shrubs and small streams, ringed by bare slopes that hold snow for half the year. Prayer flags mark a small monastery, yaks graze near the road, and a few houses and army buildings sit on the valley floor. On clear mornings the Kanchenjunga range is visible to the west from the ridges around.

Most travellers pass through on the day trip from Zuluk to Kupup. We think a night here is worth it, if everyone in your group is well and has already slept at Zuluk or Padamchen. The homestays are basic and very cold, but the evening light on the valley and the silence after dark are hard to find anywhere else in Sikkim. Indian travellers need the Silk Route permit from Rongli. Check current status before you travel.
facts: ≈ 90 km via Tsomgo or ≈ 125 km via Rongli
Yak pastures, 1888 memorials, old Baba Mandir
costs: Reserved SUV for the Silk Route
Small fee; agent may charge for arranging it

highlights.title: The open valley
highlights.text: Gnathang is one of the few broad, flat valleys on the Silk Route, at about 3,800–4,000 m. In late spring and summer it is green with grass and dotted with yaks; in October it turns gold and brown; from December it lies under snow. Walk a little way from the road for the full sweep.

highlights.title: The old Baba Mandir
highlights.text: On this side of the ridge stands the original bunker shrine of Sepoy Harbhajan Singh, who died near Nathu La in 1968. It is smaller and quieter than the newer shrine on the Nathu La road, and soldiers still keep it. Remove shoes and keep your voice low.

highlights.title: Memorials of 1888
highlights.text: Memorials along the road around Gnathang and in the nearby Tukla valley recall the British and Indian soldiers who died in the fighting of 1888, when British forces drove Tibetan troops back from Lingtu and fought them at Gnathang. They are a quiet stop for anyone interested in the frontier's history.

highlights.title: The village monastery
highlights.text: A small Buddhist monastery stands among prayer flags on the valley floor, looked after by the village. It is not a grand building, but it is the heart of Gnathang. If it is open, step in quietly and leave a small donation; if not, walk round it clockwise.

highlights.title: Yak herders and their animals
highlights.text: Families in Gnathang still keep yaks, which graze the valley and slopes in the warmer months and are moved lower when the snow comes. You may see chhurpi, the hard yak cheese, drying near houses. Keep a respectful distance from the animals and ask before photographing people.

highlights.title: Nights under the stars
highlights.text: With almost no lights and thin, dry air, Gnathang's night sky on a clear night is full of stars. It is also very cold: below freezing in most months and far below in winter. Step out for ten minutes in every layer you own, then get back under the quilts.

how_to_reach.text: Most travellers come up in an SUV hired for the Silk Route at ₹5,000–7,000 a day, via Rongli, Padamchen and Zuluk, with the permit arranged at Rongli. Gnathang is about 23 km and an hour beyond Zuluk, past Thambi View Point and Lungthung.

If the permit allows, cars can reach Gnathang from Gangtok via Tsomgo, Baba Mandir and Kupup, about 90 km, making a loop with the Rongli route. We would not sleep at Gnathang on the first night this way, because it means gaining over 2,000 m in a day.

On a tight budget, take a shared jeep from Gangtok to Rongli for ₹200–300 a seat and ask your Zuluk or Gnathang homestay to send a car from there. It takes longer and needs planning, and the homestay will usually arrange your permit if you send documents ahead.

where_to_stay: Gnathang has a few family homestays on the valley floor: simple wooden or concrete houses with small rooms, thick quilts, shared or attached bathrooms and hot water by the bucket. Dinner and breakfast are included, usually ₹1,200–2,000 per person, with rice, dal, vegetables, eggs and noodles. Rooms are very cold from October to April; ask for an extra quilt or a heater if offered. Few are listed online, so book through a Zuluk homestay or a Gangtok operator. If anyone feels unwell at this height, sleep lower at Zuluk or Padamchen instead.
tips: Do not sleep at Gnathang on your first night up; spend at least one night at Zuluk or Padamchen first.
Pack a down jacket, thermal layers, a woollen hat, gloves and thick socks for every month of the year.
Carry enough cash for the whole Silk Route, since there is no ATM beyond Rongli.
Drink plenty of water, avoid alcohol and tell your homestay if anyone develops a bad headache or breathlessness at night.
Ask before photographing army camps or soldiers, and keep to the road around military areas.

experiences.title: A night in the Gnathang valley
experiences.summary: Sleep in a family homestay in the high Gnathang valley, at about 3,800–4,000 m. Watch evening light fade over the yak pastures, eat a hot dinner by the stove and step out to a sky full of stars. Only after a night lower down, and only if everyone is well.
body: Most Silk Route travellers drive through Gnathang in the middle of the day, take photographs and head on. Staying the night changes the place. By late afternoon the day traffic is gone, the wind drops, and the valley takes on a long golden light as the sun goes down behind the western ridges. Yaks drift back towards the houses, smoke rises from kitchen chimneys and the temperature falls fast.

The homestays are simple. Expect a small room with two or three beds and a pile of quilts, a shared or attached bathroom and hot water in a bucket on request. Dinner is rice, dal, a vegetable, perhaps eggs or chicken, eaten early around the family's stove. Ask to sit in the kitchen if you can; it is the warmest room in the house and where the stories are told.

At about 3,900 m sleep can be broken, and mild headaches are common. Drink water, skip alcohol and go to bed early. If anyone develops a severe headache, vomiting, confusion or breathlessness at rest, tell your hosts and go down to Zuluk at once, even at night. In the morning, step out early: on clear days the valley is white with frost and the high ridges catch the first sun.

faqs.q: Is it safe to sleep at Gnathang?
faqs.a: For healthy adults who have already spent a night at Zuluk or Padamchen, usually yes. Sleeping at about 3,900 m on your first night up is risky. Drink water, avoid alcohol and descend at once if anyone has severe headache, vomiting, confusion or breathlessness at rest.

faqs.q: How cold is Gnathang at night?
faqs.a: Very cold. Nights are below freezing for most of the year and can fall far below in winter. Homestays provide heavy quilts, and some offer a heater for a small charge. Sleep in thermals and a woollen hat, and keep a water bottle inside your quilt so it does not freeze.

faqs.q: How do we book a homestay at Gnathang?
faqs.a: Few Gnathang homestays are listed online. Most travellers book through their Zuluk homestay, a Gangtok operator or the driver arranging the Silk Route trip. Book ahead in October, November and May. Rates are usually ₹1,200–2,000 per person with dinner and breakfast.

experiences.title: The old Baba Mandir bunker shrine
experiences.summary: On the Gnathang side of the ridge stands the original shrine of Sepoy Harbhajan Singh, a converted bunker kept by the army. It is smaller and quieter than the newer Baba Mandir on the Nathu La road, and many soldiers regard it as the true shrine.
body: Harbhajan Singh, a soldier of the Punjab Regiment, died near Nathu La on 4 October 1968. Army tradition holds that his spirit went on guarding the border, warning soldiers of danger in dreams. His first shrine was set up in a bunker on this side of the ridge, in the high country between Gnathang and Kupup, and soldiers have kept it ever since. In 1982 the army built a larger shrine on the main Nathu La road, easier for visitors to reach; this one became the old Baba Mandir.

The old shrine is reached by steps from the road. Inside are photographs, offerings and the simple furnishings of a soldier's quarters. Soldiers on duty look after it and may tell the story. As at the new shrine, visitors leave bottles of water to be blessed. Treat it as a place of worship: remove shoes, cover your head if asked, keep quiet and do not photograph where signs say not to.

The climb to the shrine is short but steep at this height, so take it slowly. Combine it with the 1888 memorials and the Elephant Lake viewpoint at Kupup on the same morning. If the weather closes in, as it often does by early afternoon, head back to Gnathang or down to Zuluk rather than waiting for the cloud to clear.

faqs.q: Where is the old Baba Mandir?
faqs.a: The old Baba Mandir is on the Silk Route side of the ridge, between Gnathang and Kupup, reached by steps from the road. It is the original bunker shrine of Sepoy Harbhajan Singh. The newer, larger shrine, built in 1982, stands on the main Gangtok–Nathu La road near Tsomgo.

faqs.q: Do we need a separate permit for the old Baba Mandir?
faqs.a: No separate permit is usually needed; the Silk Route permit that covers Zuluk, Gnathang and Kupup normally covers the old shrine on the same road. Rules can change, so confirm with your operator and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Which Baba Mandir should we visit?
faqs.a: If you are on the Silk Route, the old Baba Mandir near Gnathang is on your way and quieter. If you are on the Gangtok–Nathu La day trip, you will see the new one. Both are kept by the army and treated with equal respect, and some travellers on the loop see both.

experiences.title: The 1888 memorials around Gnathang
experiences.summary: In 1888 British forces fought Tibetan troops at Lingtu and Gnathang on this road. Memorials around Gnathang and in the nearby Tukla valley recall the soldiers who died. A quiet, short stop that explains why this valley matters to the history of the Sikkim–Tibet border.
body: In the 1880s Tibetan troops built a fort at Lingtu, on the trade road below Gnathang, inside territory the British regarded as Sikkim. In March 1888 a British force attacked and took Lingtu. On 22 May 1888 Tibetan troops attacked the British position at Gnathang and were driven off, and in September the British pushed them back over Jelep La. The Anglo-Chinese Convention of 1890 then drew the Sikkim–Tibet border along the watershed and made Sikkim a British protectorate.

Memorials along the road around Gnathang and in the Tukla valley nearby commemorate soldiers of the British and Indian forces who died in that campaign. The sites are simple, often marked by plaques and kept by the army, and drivers know where to stop. Read the inscriptions, take a moment and move on, as the wind here rarely lets up.

The memorials make most sense if you know the road. This was the Kalimpong–Lhasa trade route, and the fighting of 1888 was as much about who controlled that trade as about borders. Combine the stop with the old Baba Mandir, a memorial of a much later war, and you see how long this valley has been a frontier.

faqs.q: What happened at Gnathang in 1888?
faqs.a: During the British Sikkim expedition of 1888, Tibetan troops attacked the British position at Gnathang on 22 May and were driven back. Earlier, in March, the British had taken the Tibetan fort at Lingtu, and in September they pushed over Jelep La. The 1890 convention then fixed the Sikkim–Tibet border.

faqs.q: Where is the Tukla valley memorial?
faqs.a: The Tukla valley lies close to Gnathang on the Silk Route, and a memorial there recalls soldiers who died in the 1888 fighting. Drivers on the Zuluk–Gnathang–Kupup road know it and stop on request. It is in an army area, so follow any instructions about photography.

faqs.q: Is the memorial stop worth it?
faqs.a: Yes, if you are interested in history. It is short, usually 15–30 minutes, and on your way. It explains why this valley mattered: the fighting of 1888 decided the Sikkim–Tibet border along the watershed and opened the trade road over Jelep La to British control.

experiences.title: Yak pastures and the village monastery
experiences.summary: A slow walk from the homestays across the valley floor, past grazing yaks, chhurpi cheese drying on roofs and strings of prayer flags, to Gnathang's small monastery. It shows the village behind the Silk Route: a herding community of 13 households at nearly 4,000 m.
body: Gnathang is a herding village. Families keep yaks and yak-cattle crosses, which graze the valley floor and the slopes above in the warmer months and are taken lower when deep snow comes. From the homestays a path and the road lead across the valley, past stone walls, small streams and the animals themselves. In season you may see chhurpi, the hard yak-milk cheese, drying in strings near the houses, and butter being churned.

The small monastery sits among prayer flags on the valley floor. It is a village gompa, not a grand monastery, and is often locked when no caretaker is around. If it is open, step in quietly, take off your shoes and leave a small donation. If not, walk round it clockwise as the villagers do. Ask your homestay about the monastery's story; families here will know it better than any book.

Walk slowly. At about 3,900 m even flat ground leaves you breathless, and an hour out and back is plenty. Give yaks plenty of room, especially mothers with calves, and never walk between a herder and the animals. Ask before photographing people or houses. The best light is early morning, when frost lies on the grass and the yaks are just moving out.

faqs.q: Are yaks at Gnathang safe to approach?
faqs.a: Yaks are domestic but large and can be nervous, especially mothers with calves. Keep at least several metres away, do not walk between a herder and the animals, and never feed them. If a yak lowers its head or turns towards you, back away slowly.

faqs.q: Can we buy chhurpi at Gnathang?
faqs.a: Sometimes. Families who keep yaks make chhurpi, the hard dried cheese, and may sell a few strings if they have some to spare. Ask your homestay rather than knocking on doors. Prices are small, and it is a good, chewy snack for the road down.

faqs.q: Is the Gnathang monastery open to visitors?
faqs.a: Visitors are welcome when the caretaker is there, but the village monastery is often locked. Ask your homestay who keeps the key. If it is closed, walk round it clockwise. Remove shoes and keep quiet inside, and leave a small donation if you enter.

faqs.q: Do we need a permit for Gnathang?
faqs.a: Yes. Indian travellers need the Silk Route permit covering Zuluk, Gnathang and Kupup, issued at Rongli and usually arranged by a homestay or Gangtok operator with photo ID copies and passport photos. Foreign nationals face different and changing rules. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Gnathang the same as Nathang?
faqs.a: Yes. Gnathang, Nathang, Natang and Gnathong are all spellings of the same valley on the Silk Route between Zuluk and Kupup. Road signs, maps and booking sites use different versions, so do not be confused if your permit and your homestay spell it differently.

faqs.q: How high is Gnathang?
faqs.a: Gnathang lies at about 3,800–4,000 m, roughly 1,000 m above Zuluk. Headaches and breathlessness are common, and sleeping here on your first night up is risky. Spend at least one night at Zuluk or Padamchen before staying at Gnathang, and go down if anyone feels very unwell.

faqs.q: How far is Gnathang from Zuluk?
faqs.a: About 23 km and roughly an hour by car, climbing past Thambi View Point and Lungthung. Most Silk Route trips visit Gnathang on a day drive from Zuluk, often continuing to the old Baba Mandir and Kupup, then returning to Zuluk or going on to Gangtok via Tsomgo.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Gnathang?
faqs.a: April and May bring melting snow and longer days; October and November give clear skies and Kanchenjunga views from the ridges. December to March is very cold, with snow often closing the road. June to September is monsoon, with cloud and landslides on the way up.

faqs.q: Does it snow at Gnathang?
faqs.a: Yes, heavily. Snow usually covers the valley from about December to March and can linger into April, and falls are possible in October and November. Snow can close the road above Zuluk for days. Keep a spare day and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How much does a night at Gnathang cost?
faqs.a: Homestays charge about ₹1,200–2,000 per person a night with dinner and breakfast. An extra quilt or a heater may cost ₹100–300. The big cost of reaching Gnathang is the car, about ₹5,000–7,000 a day for an SUV on the Silk Route, so travel in a group of four to six to share it.

faqs.q: Is there mobile network at Gnathang?
faqs.a: Very weak or none. Some networks may catch a signal at points on the road, but do not count on calls or data. Tell family you will be offline for a day or two, and share your homestay's name and your driver's number before leaving Rongli.

faqs.q: Is Gnathang suitable for children and senior citizens?
faqs.a: A day visit from Zuluk suits most healthy families and fit older travellers who go slowly. Sleeping at Gnathang is harder, and we would not take infants or anyone with heart or lung problems overnight. Keep everyone warm and hydrated, and sleep lower if anyone feels unwell.
